extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in complex analysis / conformal mappings
extracted.subtask_description: Constructing and analysing conformal maps from simply connected plane regions (especially the upper half-plane or unit disc) to polygons, and the supporting technical lemmas used in the Riemann mapping theorem and Schwarz–Christoffel formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of injective holomorphic sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is a connected open subset of C and {fn} is a sequence of injective holomorphic functions on Ω that converges uniformly on every compact subset of Ω to a holomorphic function f, then f is either injective or constant (Proposition 3.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: translate so one zero is fixed, use isolated zeros and the argument principle on a small circle γ around another zero to get an integer winding number; uniform convergence on γ gives contradiction because the approximants have no zeros inside γ. Use uniform convergence on compacts and properties of zeros of holomorphic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of logarithm on simply connected region avoiding a point
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is simply connected and α ∉ Ω, then z − α never vanishes on Ω and one can define a holomorphic logarithm f(z) = log(z − α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Ω is simply connected and z−α has no zeros there, a branch of the logarithm exists; exponentiating yields ef(z)=z−α, so f is injective. Further use of the branch shows f(·) stays away from f(w)+2πi for any fixed w ∈ Ω, enabling construction of bounded injective maps into the unit disc via translation, inversion, rescaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing family F for Riemann mapping (normalization at 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F = {f : Ω → D holomorphic, injective and f(0)=0}. This family is non-empty (contains the identity after mapping Ω into D) and uniformly bounded because images lie in the unit disc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find a conformal map Ω→D fixing 0, consider supremum s = sup_{f∈F} |f'(0)| (text uses derivative at 0 in standard proof). Use Montel's theorem to extract a subsequence converging uniformly on compacts to a holomorphic limit f; Proposition 3.5 implies the non-constant limit is injective, and maximum modulus principle ensures |f(z)|<1, so f ∈ F and attains the supremum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximization + Montel + injectivity yields extremal map
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a sequence {fn} ⊂ F with |f'_n(0)| → s; by Montel, a subsequence converges uniformly on compacts to f, which is non-constant (s ≥ 1 because identity map belongs to F) and hence injective; f then attains the maximum s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard extremal-function step in the Riemann mapping theorem: Montel provides compactness, Proposition 3.5 preserves injectivity in the limit, and analytic estimates (Cauchy) bound derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjectivity via automorphisms and Schwarz lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the extremal f is onto D: if α ∈ D  (Ω), use the automorphism ψ_α of D that interchanges 0 and α, let U = (ψ_α ∘ f)(Ω) (simply connected, does not contain 0), define a square root g on U, then form F = ψ_{g(α)} ∘ g ∘ ψ_α ∘ f; F ∈ F but yields |F'(0)|>|f'(0)|, contradicting maximality unless f is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key ingredients: automorphisms of the disc, existence of branch (square root) on simply connected domains avoiding 0, composition producing a new function in F with larger derivative at 0, and the last-part Schwarz lemma which forces strict inequality for non-injective Φ mapping D→D with Φ(0)=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holomorphically simply connected suffices for log/sqrt
rubrics_metrics.description: The only uses of simple connectivity in the Riemann mapping proof were to define logarithm and square root; it suffices to assume Ω is holomorphically simply connected (i.e., ∫_γ f(z)dz = 0 for every holomorphic f and closed curve γ in Ω).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This weaker hypothesis ensures multi-valued functions like log and sqrt have single-valued branches when needed. Appendix B discussed equivalent properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and branch choice for Schwarz–Christoffel integral
rubrics_metrics.description: S(z) = ∫_0^z dζ / ∏_{k=1}^n (ζ − A_k)^{β_k}, where A1 < A2 < ... < An are distinct real points and each factor (z−A_k)^{β_k} is the branch cut in the plane slit along the ray {A_k + i y : y ≤ 0} that is positive for real x>A_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify slit-plane branches so integrand is holomorphic off the downward rays; the integral can be taken along any path avoiding the slits. Continuity up to the real line (including A_k) requires β_k<1 so (ζ−A_k)^{−β_k} is integrable near A_k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability near vertices (β_k < 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each exponent β_k must satisfy β_k < 1 so that the singularities (ζ − A_k)^{−β_k} are integrable near A_k and S is continuous up to the real line including the points A_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guarantees S(z) has finite boundary values at the A_k and that the integral defining S converges near those points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence at infinity (sum β_k > 1) and definition of a_∞
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume ∑_{k=1}^n β_k > 1 so that for large |ζ| the integrand decays like |ζ|^{-∑ β_k} and the integral (5) converges at infinity; then lim_{r→∞} S(r e^{iθ}) exists and is independent of θ; denote this limit a_∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition is used to ensure S has a finite image for the point at infinity and to control behavior on the unbounded real half-segments. (Text phrases this in terms of the decay inequality and then calls the limit a_∞.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygon theorem (sum β_k = 2 gives closed polygon)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑_{k=1}^n β_k = 2 and p has vertices a_k = S(A_k) in order, then S maps the real axis onto p \{a_∞}, where a_∞ lies on segment [a_n, a_1] and is the image of the point at infinity. The interior angle at vertex a_k is α_k π where α_k = 1 − β_k (Proposition 4.1(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the argument of S'(x) on intervals (A_k, A_{k+1}) to see each interval maps to a straight segment; the change in direction across vertices is π β_k, hence interior angle πα_k. If 1 < ∑ β_k < 2, a_∞ becomes an additional vertex and the polygon has n+1 sides (Proposition 4.1(ii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle computation via S'(x) argument
rubrics_metrics.description: For A_k < x < A_{k+1}, S'(x) = ∏_{j≤k} (x−A_j)^{−β_j} ∏_{j>k} (x−A_j)^{−β_j} so arg S'(x) = −π ∑_{j>k} β_j (constant on that interval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence as x moves across successive intervals the image segments have constant directions and the cumulative change yields the polygonal turning angles; this computational rule gives explicit geometric correspondence between β_k and side directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two caveats for S being conformal map to a given polygon
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) For generic choices of A_1,...,A_n the image polygon can self-intersect, so S may not produce a simple polygon; 2) Proposition 4.1 does not guarantee that for a given simply connected polygonal region P there exist A_k so that S is conformal from H onto P without further adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus one must choose the preimages A_k carefully (and possibly modify the integral) to obtain a one-to-one conformal map to a prescribed polygonal region; later theorems address existence and normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary continuity of conformal maps to polygons (Theorem 4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F : D → P is a conformal map (P a polygonal region), then F extends to a continuous bijection from the closed disc D̄ to the closure P̄; in particular, F induces a bijection between ∂D and the polygon boundary p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main task is to show radial limits exist at each boundary point; this uses area estimates, Cauchy-Schwarz, and the finiteness of Area(P) to rule out persistent image separation on small boundary circles (see Lemmas 4.3–4.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area change formula for conformal maps
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : U → f(U) is conformal, then Area(f(U)) = ∫_U |f'(z)|^2 dx dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identity follows from the Jacobian determinant of the change of variables w = f(z) being |f'(z)|^2; it's used in the proof of boundary behavior lemmas (notably Lemma 4.3) to relate boundary arc integrals to the bounded area of P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma ensuring images along some radii shrink (Lemma 4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a boundary point z_0 on ∂D and for each small r a pair of points z_r, z'_r on the circle C_r (centered at z_0 of radius r) inside D, define ρ(r)=|f(z_r)−f(z'_r)|. Then there exists a sequence r_n→0 with ρ(r_n)→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume ρ(r)≥c>0 for small r, parametrize the arc between z_r and z'_r, apply Cauchy-Schwarz to bound ρ(r) in terms of ∫_{arc} |f'|^2, square and divide by r, integrate in r to get left side divergent (∫ dr/r) but right side finite (Area bound), contradiction. This lemma is a key technical device for proving boundary limits exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of boundary limits for conformal map (Lemma 4.4 and 4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For z_0 ∈ ∂D, F(z) tends to a limit as z→z_0 within D; defining F(z_0) as that limit yields a continuous extension of F to the closed disc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contradict any two distinct cluster values by producing two disjoint boundary neighborhoods and preimage curves whose intersections with small circles violate Lemma 4.3; then show continuity up to boundary by standard ε–δ arguments and applying the same reasoning to the inverse map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz reflection and strip continuation for local power map hk
rubrics_metrics.description: Near a vertex a_k with interior angle α_k π, define h_k(z) = (F(z) − a_k)^{1/α_k} in an appropriate half-strip so that h_k maps a real segment to a straight segment and extends by Schwarz reflection to an analytic function in the full strip Re z ∈ (A_{k-1}, A_{k+1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because F maps adjacent real segments to straight segments meeting at angle πα_k, the local 1/α_k power straightens the corner; Schwarz reflection across the real axis then analytically continues h_k to the whole strip. Nonvanishing of h'_k is argued from conformality and injectivity, which is used to control F' near A_k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logarithmic derivative identity leading to SC integrand
rubrics_metrics.description: For a conformal F mapping H→P with F(A_k)=a_k, one obtains globally F''(z)/F'(z) = −∑_{k=1}^n β_k/(z − A_k), where β_k = 1 − α_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from local analysis in overlapping strips and analytic continuation; the right-hand side is entire except for the simple poles at A_k and decays at infinity, so by Liouville the difference is zero. Integrating gives F'(z) = c ∏_{k=1}^n (z − A_k)^{−β_k}, and integrating again yields the Schwarz–Christoffel formula F = c1 ∫ Q + c2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz–Christoffel formula for conformal maps to polygon (Theorem 4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist constants c1 and c2 so that the conformal map F of H to P is given by F(z) = c1 S(z) + c2 where S is the Schwarz–Christoffel integral S(z)=∫_0^z dζ ∏_{k=1}^n (ζ−A_k)^{−β_k}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization constants c1, c2 determined by mapping specific preimages to chosen vertices. The proof uses the logarithmic derivative identity, Liouville's theorem, and integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variant when infinity maps to a vertex (Theorem 4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F maps A_1,...,A_{n-1},∞ to the vertices of p, then F(z) = C1 ∫_0^z dζ / ∏_{k=1}^{n-1} (ζ−A_k)^{β_k} + C2; equivalently, delete the last term in the SC integral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: precompose F with a Möbius automorphism Φ of H sending ∞ to a finite point A_n, apply the previous SC formula to F◦Φ^{-1}, then change variables ζ=Φ(w) (dζ = dw/w^2) and use β_1+...+β_n = 2 to simplify; finally undo Φ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic integral as special SC case and normalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The elliptic integral I(z)=∫_0^z dζ/[(1−ζ^2)(1−k^2 ζ^2)]^{1/2} (0<k<1) maps H conformally onto a rectangle R with vertices ±K, ±K+iK', for appropriate complete elliptic integrals K(k),K'(k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By Theorem 4.6 and symmetry, choose normalizations mapping −1,0,1 to −K,0,K and determine the remaining constant by comparing K(k)/K'(k) monotonicity to show the scalar c1=1. The inverse sn(z) is then doubly periodic (periods 4K and 2iK') and has only poles—an elliptic function.
